title: Excited delirium the focus of jury's findings
article: A coroner's jury has made recommendations about how police officers, paramedics and hospital emergency room staff deal with people exhibiting symptoms of being "medically excited."
The jury recommended that paramedics and emergency room personnel receive more training in recognizing the signs and symptoms of excited delirium, as well as in the management of the condition.
And that police officers receive training in excited delirium both in initial recruit training and during refresher training they take every three years.

As well, the three men and two women recommended the RCMP develop a specific standalone national policy in recognizing and managing persons with excited delirium, and suggested police officers should always ride with an ambulance carrying a person identified as exhibiting signs of excited delirium.
In addition, they also said research money should be allocated to looking into the cause and effect of excited delirium.
The recommendations came late Wednesday, after jurors heard almost two days of testimony in an inquest into the death of 27-year-old Colin Kenson Tremeer.

Tremeer had left his Kelowna home early on the morning of Aug. 5 after arguing with his girlfriend, and flagged down an ambulance downtown, telling paramedic Jo Ann Hubbard that someone was trying to kill him.
Hubbard already had a patient on board that she was taking to Kelowna hospital, so she contacted her dispatcher, who called RCMP at 5:16 a.m.
Police were dispatched three minutes later, but didn't find Tremeer until 5:31 a.m., standing in the middle of Highway 97 in the downtown core.
Tremeer jumped into the back of the police cruiser when officers found him, and told them he needed help because someone was trying to kill him.
The officers decided to take Tremeer, who was sweating and flailing about, to the RCMP station as they felt it was the safest place to figure out how to help him.
En route, Const. Jordan McLellan noticed Tremeer's feet were injured and said he seemed to drift in and out of "his own little world."

When they reached the RCMP station at 5:34 a.m. and removed Tremeer from the police cruiser, McLellan said he thought he may be dealing with something beyond intoxication and thought Tremeer, 27, might be suffering from excited delirium.
That's when, at 5:36 a.m., he radioed his dispatcher to request ambulance personnel come to the detachment to treat Tremeer.
At 5:38 a.m., B.C. Ambulance Service was contacted by RCMP dispatcher, and officers left the detachment to follow the ambulance carrying Tremeer to hospital at 5:55 a.m.
On the way, paramedics pulled over and a police officer was brought on board to help keep Tremeer under control while paramedics treated him, as his limbs were flailing around.
Const. Dylan Hardy said Tremeer appeared "more afraid than anything."

Jurors also heard that excited delirium is discussed in some RCMP training and policies, but there is not a specific policy dealing solely with excited delirium, which Dr. Christine Hall says refers to a person who is delirious and "medically excited."
However, she added it is a condition, not a diagnosis, as there are a number of things that could cause someone to exhibit those symptoms, including ingestion of drugs.

Tremeer died in hospital on Aug. 5, and jurors have concluded his death was caused by cardiac arrest due to cocaine overdose. He also had an enlarged heart, which they listed as a contributing factor, along with excited delirium.
The death has been classified as accidental.
